newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: APEC - Cigar-loving Ramos welcomes leaders.
newsitem.headline: APEC - Cigar-loving Ramos welcomes leaders.

text.p: Philippine President Fidel Ramos gripped a fat cigar, leaders of Asia-Pacific economies tried gamely -- but failed -- to do a "Mexican wave", and the fashion statement was the Barong shirt.
Woven from silk and pineapple fibres, the Barong became the trademark of the fourth Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Monday in Subic Bay.
The picturesque bay was once a U.S. naval base where American fleets sheltered from typhoons.

U.S. President Bill Clinton playfully began a rippling, hands-above-the-head "Mexican wave" as heads of 18 APEC economies lined up at the end of a red carpet on a manicured lawn for their official photo.
But it was all too much for the likes of Indonesian President Suharto, South Korean President Kim Young-sam and Sir Julius Chan of Papua New Guinea.
"No, no," groaned Clinton as the wave crashed in a jumble of arms.
Ramos is a reformed smoker. But he's rarely without an unlit cigar clamped in his teeth.

Every bit the suave host, Ramos squeezed a long cigar between two fingers of one hand and gestured expansively across Subic Bay with the other as he personally welcomed each leader for the summit inside a former American officers' club.
The Barong -- a loosely fitting shirt worn outside the trousers -- caused problems for some of the leaders of half of humanity.
Ramos patiently explained to his guests that the top button should be undone. He personally tugged open the collar of Chinese President Jiang Zemin.
Thai Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa, looking gloomy despite the picture-perfect sunny day, was having none of it. His Barong stayed tightly buttoned.

Banharn had other things on his mind. After losing an election he looked like being replaced even before the summit breaks up. At home, the Thai stock market was bubbling cheerfully at the prospect of his departure.
Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, often branded a maverick in APEC trade talks, was the only leader not sporting black trousers to set off his pressed white smock -- his were charcoal grey.

In its heyday during the Vietnam War, there were some wild goings-on at the officer's club, one of the most popular military watering holes in the Pacific. But it crumbled into disrepair after the Philippines kicked the Americans out in 1991.
Now it's the gleaming centre-piece of a country club that boasts a golf course carved out of jungle-clad hills inhabited by chattering monkeys.
Renovations were going on until the final moments, and the whiff of fresh paint hung in the summit hall as the leaders strode across an off-white carpet to their seats.
Arranged in an horse-shoe shape, with Ramos in the middle and Clinton and Austrialian Prime Minister John Howard at opposite far ends, the chairs were sheathed in white slip covers.
No conference table separated the leaders -- beside each chair was a small table with a microphone on top.

To preserve the moment for posterity, a chest filled with summit momentos offered by each country -- including golf balls from the Philippines and a bottle of Australian vintage wine -- was parked in a corner.
The APEC time capsule is to be deposited in the Philippines National Museum.
